slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content:
Wine is a product of nature, and climate is one of the most critical natural factors shaping a wine's style. Bordeaux enjoys a uniquely favourable temperate oceanic climate — warm but not hot, humid but not excessive, with distinct seasons that change gradually. These climatic conditions create an ideal growing environment for Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, and other grape varieties.

This course will take you deep into Bordeaux's climate and environmental characteristics. We will learn about the causes and features of the temperate oceanic climate, the moderating effects of the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf Stream, the protective role of the pine forests, and key climatic data including annual average temperature, rainfall, and sunshine hours. Most importantly, we will understand how these climatic factors influence the grape-growing cycle and fruit quality.

Learning Objectives

🌡️ Master Bordeaux's Climatic Characteristics

Understand the definition, features, and advantages of a temperate oceanic climate

🌊 Learn the Ocean Moderation Mechanism

Understand how the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf Stream influence Bordeaux's temperature and humidity

🌲 Understand the Role of Topography and Vegetation

Learn how the pine-forest belt protects vineyards from sea winds and salt spray

📊 Analyse Climatic Data

Master key figures such as annual average temperature, rainfall, and sunshine hours, and their significance for viticulture

🍇 Understand the Climate–Grape Connection

Learn how different climatic conditions affect the sugar level, acidity, tannins, and flavour of grapes

After completing this course, you will be able to describe Bordeaux's climatic characteristics professionally and understand how climate shapes the unique style of Bordeaux wine.

slides.3.title: Temperate Oceanic Climate — Temperature Characteristics
slides.3.description: Based on 30-year average data from the Bordeaux-Mérignac weather station (1991–2020)
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Mild Climate
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Annual average temperature 12.7°C; growing season warm but not hot
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Stable Variation
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Winter 6°C, summer 21°C — a moderate temperature range
slides.3.quiz.question: What is the average temperature range during Bordeaux's growing season (April–October)?
slides.3.quiz.explanation: During Bordeaux's growing season (April–October) temperatures range approximately 11.5–20.7°C. This range allows grapes to ripen slowly and steadily, which is conducive to the development of flavour compounds.
slides.4.title: Temperate Oceanic Climate — Rainfall Characteristics
slides.4.description: Annual rainfall approximately 885 mm; more rainfall in autumn and winter
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Rainy Autumn
slides.4.highlights.0.content: October–November sees the highest rainfall; careful harvest management is essential
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Dry Summer
slides.4.highlights.1.content: June–August rainfall is lower; supplemental irrigation may be required
slides.4.quiz.question: Which season receives the most rainfall in Bordeaux?
slides.4.quiz.explanation: Bordeaux receives the most rainfall in autumn (October–November), reaching 95–110 mm. This is a significant challenge for harvest management and requires precisely timing the pick.

slides.6.title: Temperate Oceanic Climate — Sunshine and Humidity
slides.6.description: Ample sunshine promotes the accumulation of grape sugars and flavour development

slides.6.highlights.0.content: July achieves 240 hours of sunshine; photosynthesis is at its most vigorous
slides.6.highlights.1.title: Annual Total
slides.6.highlights.1.content: Approximately 1,790 hours per year, meeting the needs of premium viticulture
slides.6.quiz.question: Which month in Bordeaux has the most sunshine hours?
slides.6.quiz.explanation: July has the most sunshine hours in Bordeaux, reaching approximately 240 hours. This abundant sunlight drives photosynthesis and promotes sugar accumulation and the development of flavour compounds in the grapes.

slides.10.title: Risks and Responses
slides.10.subtitle: Climatic Challenges and Management Strategies
slides.11.title: Climate Risk Checklist and Response Strategies
slides.11.highlights.0.title: Climatic Challenges
slides.11.highlights.0.content: Spring frost, summer drought, autumn rainfall, and other hazards
slides.11.highlights.1.title: Countermeasures
slides.11.highlights.1.content: Risk management combining modern technology with traditional knowledge
slides.11.content:
Although Bordeaux's climate is broadly suitable for viticulture, it still faces multiple climatic risks that require careful management.

❄️ Spring Frost Risk

Risk: Frost can still occur in April, damaging new shoots and flowers

Impact: Reduces the year's yield; severe cases may cause total crop loss

Countermeasures:

  • Frost candles or heaters
  • Sprinkler systems (ice-layer protection)
  • Delayed pruning strategy
  • Frost-resistant varieties or rootstocks

☀️ Summer Drought and Heat Waves

Risk: Extreme heat and drought affect vine development

Impact: Premature ripening, acidity loss, flavour imbalance

Countermeasures:

  • Precision irrigation systems
  • Canopy management (partial shading)
  • Mulch to retain soil moisture
  • Drought-tolerant rootstocks

🌧️ Autumn Rainfall Risk

Risk: Rain during harvest causes berry swelling and disease

Impact: Dilutes sugars, increases disease risk, affects wine quality

Countermeasures:

  • Precise maturity monitoring
  • Rapid harvest decision-making
  • Staggered picking strategy
  • Optical sorting technology

🦠 Disease Pressure

Risk: Humid climate encourages fungal disease

Impact: Mildew, powdery mildew, and other diseases affect yield and quality

Countermeasures:

  • Preventive spraying (organic or conventional)
  • Canopy management to promote airflow
  • Disease-resistant variety selection
  • Biological control methods

▲ Winter pruning technique demonstration

▲ Common pest and disease identification guide

🌍 Climate Change Adaptation Strategies

  • Variety adjustment: Introduce heat-tolerant varieties or adjust blending ratios
  • Harvest timing: Pick earlier to preserve acidity and freshness
  • Irrigation management: Precision control of water stress
  • Vineyard aspect: Select cooler exposures or higher elevations
  • Technological innovation: Use weather stations, satellite monitoring, and other modern tools
slides.12.title: Why Does Merlot Ripen Earlier?
slides.12.highlights.0.title: Earlier Phenological Timing
slides.12.highlights.0.content: Merlot's budbreak and véraison are generally earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon
slides.12.highlights.1.title: Sugar–Acid Dynamics
slides.12.highlights.1.content: Sugar accumulation is faster and acidity drops earlier
slides.12.content:
Merlot is one of Bordeaux's most important grape varieties. Its relatively early-ripening character makes it especially well-suited to certain appellations and climatic conditions.

🌸 Growth Cycle Characteristics

  • Budbreak: Approximately 1 week earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Flowering: Earlier flowering with a longer pollination window
  • Véraison: Colour change begins late July to early August
  • Harvest: Typically mid-September, 2–3 weeks ahead of Cabernet Sauvignon

🧬 Varietal Physiological Traits

  • Thinner skin: More easily accumulates sugar, but also more susceptible to disease
  • Larger berries: Higher water content; relatively lower sugar concentration
  • Rapid acidity loss: Acidity drops faster during the ripening phase
  • Softer tannins: Lower tannin content that is more supple

🌍 Climatic Adaptability

  • Right Bank advantage: Clay soils retain moisture well, suiting Merlot
  • Cooler areas: Early-ripening trait allows maturation in cooler appellations
  • Frost risk: Early budbreak increases exposure to spring frost
  • Harvest window: Greater chance of completing harvest before autumn rains

🍷 Flavour and Quality Impact

  • Fruit-forward: Dark fruit (plum, blackberry) and red fruit aromas
  • Supple palate: Soft tannins, rounded body
  • Approachable young: Can be enjoyed early without extended ageing
  • Blending role: Adds suppleness and fruit character to blends

💡 Key Summary
🍇 Merlot Strengths
  • ✓ Early ripening suits cooler climates
  • ✓ Avoids autumn rainfall risk
  • ✓ Supple and approachable

🍷 Cabernet Sauvignon Strengths
  • ✓ Late budbreak avoids frost
  • ✓ Thick skin resists disease
  • ✓ Powerful structure and ageing potential
  • ✓ Outstanding on gravel soils

🌱 Key Viticulture Management Points

  • Frost protection: Early budbreak demands stronger spring frost protection measures
  • Yield control: Prone to overcropping; strict cluster thinning is essential
  • Harvest timing: Monitor maturity precisely; avoid overripening and acidity loss
  • Disease management: Thin skin is disease-prone; preventive management is key
slides.12.quiz.question: What is the main early-ripening characteristic of Merlot compared to Cabernet Sauvignon?
slides.12.quiz.explanation: Merlot is typically harvested in mid-September, about 2–3 weeks ahead of Cabernet Sauvignon. This early-ripening character allows it to be picked before autumn rains arrive, reducing climatic risk.
slides.13.title: Lesson Complete
slides.13.description: Congratulations on completing the foundational study of Bordeaux varieties and blending! You have now mastered the key characteristics of Bordeaux's five principal red varieties (Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, and Malbec) and its white varieties (Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, and Muscadelle). More importantly, you understand Bordeaux's distinctive blending philosophy — combining different varieties to balance risk, increase complexity, and create a more perfect wine.
